content: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and entecavir (ETV) are approved antiviral treatments for children with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). TDF is approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for children aged two years and older with CHB, and by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for children aged two years and older who weigh at least 10 kg. Entecavir (ETV) is approved for children aged two years and older. Tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) is approved by the EMA for children aged six years and older who weigh more than 25 kg, and by the FDA for children aged 12 years and older with compensated liver disease. Globally, CHB is most prevalent in the African region, with more than 80% of children under five years of age with CHB residing in 16 countries. Four countries—Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Indonesia, and Nigeria—account for 57% of the global burden. A systematic review of studies from Western Africa up to 2019 found a 5% prevalence of hepatitis B among children and adolescents under 16 years, with higher rates in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Western Africa (9%). CHB is rare among children and adolescents in North America and Western Europe, although prevalence is increasing among migrants from high-prevalence regions. Vertical mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) is the most common mode of hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmission globally, with approximately 8 million new infections annually among children under five years. Horizontal transmission (child-to-child or intrafamilial) is particularly common in sub-Saharan Africa due to poor infection control and unsafe injection practices in healthcare and traditional settings. Data on HBV acquisition among adolescents who inject drugs or engage in high-risk sexual behaviors are limited. The 2015 WHO hepatitis B guidelines did not include specific treatment recommendations for children or adolescents due to limited trial data, low curative response rates requiring long-term therapy, and concerns about long-term safety and drug resistance. At that time, ETV was the only approved treatment for children under 12 years. A conservative approach to treatment was recommended unless specific criteria, such as cirrhosis or severe necroinflammatory disease, were met. Recent studies have provided additional data on antiviral drugs for children and adolescents, leading to updated 2024 WHO guidelines that expand and simplify treatment eligibility, aligning recommendations for adolescents with those for adults. The updated guidelines recommend treatment for adolescents aged 12–17 years with CHB based on conditional evidence, except for those with significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, for whom treatment is strongly recommended. Antiviral therapy for children under 12 years remains on a case-by-case basis due to limited evidence. Preferred treatments for adolescents include tenofovir (TDF or TAF) or entecavir (ETV), with TAF considered an alternative for adolescents aged 12 years and older weighing more than 35 kg. A systematic review of 13 studies (12 randomized controlled trials) on children and adolescents with CHB found that most studies focused on those with very high baseline viral loads (>2 million IU/mL). Treatment outcomes included ALT normalization, HBeAg seroconversion, and HBV DNA suppression, but no studies reported clinical outcomes such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) or cirrhosis. Evidence for treatment efficacy in adolescents is limited, with most data extrapolated from adult studies showing that antiviral therapy reduces fibrosis progression, cirrhosis, and HCC incidence. Non-invasive tests for liver fibrosis, such as transient elastography and APRI, have been evaluated in children and adolescents with CHB, but thresholds for diagnosing significant fibrosis or cirrhosis differ from those for adults. Studies have primarily involved children undergoing liver biopsy, likely representing a subgroup with higher fibrosis prevalence. Recommendations for adolescents are based on extrapolated adult data. The balance of benefits and harms for expanding treatment to adolescents with CHB was considered in the context of limited evidence and short-duration trials. Strong recommendations for treating adolescents with significant fibrosis or cirrhosis are based on indirect evidence from adult studies showing substantial benefits outweighing harms. Conditional recommendations for other treatment eligibility criteria reflect weaker evidence for adolescents and a narrower balance of benefits to harms.
